This the type of question that faces a common problem in astronomy. i.e. We have a very limited sample size to work with.

Although we've found planets orbiting other stars, most of planets we've found have been gas giants, even among the rocky worlds, the vast majority are much larger than Earth. This isn't because small earthllike planets don't exist, it's because we can barely see them with our current telescope technology (it's much easier to see something big). And if finding something the size of Earth is difficult, trying to find a moon is even harder.

So if we look at the planets we do have solid information on, Mercury has no moons, Venus has no moons, Mars has two moons, but they appear to be captured asteroids. (I'm excluding gas giants here because they don't have a 'surface' to stand on.)

Earth does have a moon, which was formed from the same material as the planet, early during it's formation. We have a sample size of one. Any answer you get is going to be based on a lot of assumptions and extrapolations, any of which could be wrong.

But, if we look at Earth it has several interesting features.

First of all, it's in the Suns Goldilocks zone, if it wasn't in the Goldilocks zone it wouldn't support life and you wouldn't be asking this question (anthropic principle). Basically, the bigger a star is the hotter it is, which means the further away the Goldilocks zone is. The further away a star is, the smaller the star will look from it's surface. i.e. A habitable planet will orbit a small star closely, or a big star from far away. The net result is that the apparent size of the star will stay within a narrow set of ranges.

Secondly, big moons may be necessary for the development of intelligent life. This is a wonderful gif that shows the moon diverting a piece of space junk away from Earth. The moon also has many more impact craters on it's dark side than it does on it's near side, implying that the moon has been hit by many asteroids etc that would have otherwise hit Earth. Constant bombardment by asteroids would've made it very difficult for intelligent life to arise on Earth.

So for a planet to develop life, and intelligent life, it may well be necessary for it to have a moon with a similar apparent size as it's host star.

A final additional fact worth pointing out is that the moon hasn't always had the same apparent size. The moon is very slowly moving away from Earth due to tidal forces the apparent size of the moon a billion years ago would have been noticeably bigger, a billion years from now it will be noticeably smaller.
